name: rmdir
description: Removes empty directories only — the safe, deliberate alternative to rm -r.

flags.description: Remove the directory and its parents if they become empty (e.g. rmdir -p a/b/c removes c, then b, then a).
--verbose: print a message for each directory removed.
Do not report an error if a directory is not empty (still exits nonzero in some implementations).

examples.explanation: Deletes old-dir only if it contains nothing. If it has any file, rmdir refuses.

examples.command: rmdir: failed to remove 'old-dir': Directory not empty
examples.output: rmdir: failed to remove 'old-dir': Directory not empty
examples.explanation: This refusal is the whole point: rmdir cannot destroy data, unlike rm -r.
Creates a nested path and then removes the entire empty chain: c, then b, then a.
Verbose mode confirms each removal — useful in cleanup scripts.

about: rmdir calls the rmdir(2) system call, which the kernel only honors for empty directories. Where rm -r deletes trees, rmdir is a scalpel: it fails loudly on anything containing files, making it safe for scripted cleanup where you only want to prune empty structure.
A common shell pattern is rmdir -p $(dirname "$f") after moving the last file out of a directory tree.
useCases: Prune empty directory chains after moving files out.
Delete directories safely when you are not sure they are empty — rmdir will refuse rather than destroy data.
Clean up empty work directories in scripts.
mistakes: Using rmdir on a directory with hidden files (.bashrc counts as content) and being surprised it fails.
Reaching for rm -rf out of habit when rmdir would do the job safely.
warnings: None significant — rmdir cannot delete non-empty directories, which is precisely its safety feature.
distroNotes: Part of GNU coreutils on Linux; behavior is identical on BSD/macOS since it maps directly to the POSIX rmdir(2) call.
